title: The Theban alphabet
otherNames: alphabetum Honorii cognomento Thebani, 'the alphabet of Honorius surnamed the Theban' (Trithemius, Polygraphia, 1518, as quoted in secondary sources)
Runes of Honorius (modern; the signs are not runes)
the witches' alphabet / Witch's alphabet (modern Wiccan and popular usage)
family: A secret alphabet keyed to Latin: one invented sign for each letter of the Latin alphabet, in Latin order. It was printed among Trithemius's cipher alphabets and among Agrippa's characters of spirits. It is NOT one of the Hebrew-keyed ring-letter alphabets (Celestial, Malachim, Transitus fluvii) of Agrippa III.30.
summary: A secret alphabet of 23 signs, one for each Latin letter from A to Z (I also serves for J and V for U; there is no W), followed by a final sign. It first appears in print in Johannes Trithemius's Polygraphia (July 1518). Trithemius presents it as the alphabet of 'Honorius surnamed the Theban' and names Pietro d'Abano as his witness, but no surviving work attributed to d'Abano is known to contain it. Agrippa reprinted it with the same attribution in De occulta philosophia, Book III, chapter 29 (1533). It passed through Barrett's Magus (1801) into modern occultism, and Wiccans now often call it 'the witches' alphabet'.

firstAttestation.work: Polygraphiae libri sex Ioannis Trithemii abbatis Peapolitani, quondam Spanheimensis, ad Maximilianum Caesarem
firstAttestation.author: Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), formerly abbot of Sponheim, from 1506 abbot of St Jakob (the Schottenkloster) at Würzburg (GND record; SEP). A Source Library note glosses the title's 'abbatis Peapolitani' as 'abbot of Würzburg'; the etymology of the Latin form was not confirmed.
firstAttestation.date: July 1518. The Library of Congress record transcribes the imprint as 'anno a Christo nato MDXVIII men. Iulio'; the Folger record as 'anno MDXVIII mense Iulio'. The UVaDoc record notes that both parts have colophons and takes the publication data from the second (sig. C3v). The book appeared after Trithemius's death in December 1516. Composition: an NSA Center for Cryptologic History pamphlet says he began writing it at Würzburg in 1508; German Wikipedia (read via Wikiwand) says it was completed in 1508; the publisher's description of Maximilian Gamer's edition (Brill, 2022) says Trithemius dedicated it to Maximilian I in 1508 and handed over an autograph of this first, manuscript version. 'Begun' and 'completed' in 1508 are different claims; give both.
firstAttestation.place: Disputed between Basel and Oppenheim. The colophon names the bookseller Johannes Haselberg 'de Aia', of the diocese of Constance ('Constantiensis Dioecesis'), at whose cost ('aere ac impensis') it was printed (Folger transcription); the Folger record says Haselberg was active at Reichenau 1515–1537. The Folger record says it was printed chiefly by Michael Furter of Basel, who died between 5 March and 2 May 1517, and reports that Panzer, Brunet, Grässe, Caillet, LC and Shulman give Oppenheim, while Isaac, Dodgson, BM STC and Wellcome give A. Petri, Basel. The Wellcome record reads '[Basle]: A. Petri for J. Haselberger de Aia'; the Metropolitan Museum names Adam Petri as printer; a Christie's lot gives Oppenheim, Jakob Köbel; the current Library of Congress record gives Basel; the UVaDoc record reports that ICCU places Haselberg in Basel in 1518–19 rather than Oppenheim. Woodcuts: the Met credits Hans Springinklee; the Folger notes that Dodgson gives the title woodcut to Springinklee and M. Lankorońska (Gutenberg-Jahrbuch 1955, p. 111) to an artist of Burgkmair's workshop (the 'Petrarcameister').
firstAttestation.locator:
NOT VERIFIED for the 1518 printing: no book, folio or signature was seen, and the sources disagree.
(a) Peterson (The Sworn Book of Honorius, introduction) cites 'Johannes Trithemius, Polygraphia 6, 1508, p. 579', i.e. Book VI. His '1508' is the composition date; the paginated edition he used is not named in what I saw.
(b) Wikipedia's 'The Sworn Book of Honorius' cites p. 597. Freeman Presson's blog (2014, a hobby source) ties p. 597 to the 1613 Zetzner (Strasbourg) edition with Adolphus von Glauburg's notes. 579 and 597 may be one figure transposed.
(c) Neither page number can be a page of the 1518 printing, which is unpaginated and runs to about 255–270 leaves (Pandolfini: [255] leaves; UVaDoc: [268] leaves; ABAA: (270) ff.). They fit the paginated Zetzner octavo (1600: 612 pp., Czech library record) or its 1613 reprint. This is an inference from the collations, not a reading of the page.
(d) In the 1561 French translation the Theban page is fol. 184v (Wikimedia Commons scan of the Boston Public Library copy on the Internet Archive). A Wikipedia talk-page editor calls it 'page 184, Book V'; the book number was not confirmed.
(e) The ABAA bookseller's placing of the alphabets in Book V could not be seen in the search snippet and is unconfirmed. Book VI (Peterson) and Book V (talk page, for the French) remain in conflict.
firstAttestation.notes: The earliest exemplar reported by the sources consulted (Wikipedia; Peterson); no earlier print is known. CAUTION: Trithemius's first, manuscript version of the Polygraphia (1508; critical edition by Maximilian Gamer, Brill, 2022) was not checked for the Theban table. If it has the table, the first attestation is the 1508 manuscript, not the 1518 print. Trithemius introduces the table as 'another alphabet of Honorius surnamed the Theban', with which Honorius hid his 'follies in magic', 'as Petrus de Apono testifies in his greater fourth book' (Latin known only through Peterson and other secondary quotations; see quotations). Peterson: 'I have not been able to identify any such passage in the many voluminous works of De Abano'. The alphabet is not in the Liber iuratus Honorii manuscripts, with one exception reported by Wikipedia and Peterson: the composite BL Sloane MS 3853, which names Agrippa as its source. The 1561 French version, as rendered in English on its Wikimedia Commons page, says Honorius used the alphabet to set down his rules and ordinances of magic secretly, and does not name d'Abano.

transmission.author: Johannes Trithemius
transmission.what: Written at Würzburg. An NSA Center for Cryptologic History pamphlet says Trithemius began it in 1508; German Wikipedia says he completed it then; the publisher's description of Gamer's 2022 edition says he dedicated it to Maximilian I in 1508 and handed over an autograph. That first, manuscript version differs from the 1518 printing (Gamer). Publication was delayed until after his death; History of Information gives ecclesiastical disapproval as the cause. Whether the 1508 manuscript already contains the Theban table was NOT checked.

transmission.work: Polygraphiae libri sex ([Basel or Oppenheim], at the expense of Johannes Haselberg)
transmission.author: Johannes Trithemius
transmission.what: The first printing. The alphabet is presented as the one with which 'Honorius surnamed the Theban' hid his magical follies, with Petrus de Apono's 'greater fourth book' cited as witness. The table runs A to Z on the Latin order and ends with a sign that a Wikipedia talk-page editor and From Old Books report is labelled 'w'.

transmission.date: 1533 (July 1533, from the colophon per the McGill record)
transmission.work: De occulta philosophia libri tres ([Cologne: J. Soter?]; Adams suggests Basel; four or five issues of this date)
transmission.author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim (1486–1535)
transmission.what: Book III, chapter 29, which the 1651 English heads 'Of the Characters and Seals of spirits' (Peterson's transcription). Agrippa sets the alphabet among the secret characters, as figures that Peter of Abano ('Peter Apponus' in the 1651 English; the 1533 Latin form was not checked) notes as delivered by Honorius of Thebes. He follows Trithemius, and Peterson's edition annotates the chapter with the Polygraphia passage. As reported by From Old Books (and Wikipedia's caption), the final sign here carries a small ω at its foot and the label Ω; most later charts copy this version. Wikipedia calls Agrippa Trithemius's 'student'. The documented contact is Agrippa's visit to Trithemius at St Jakob, Würzburg, in the winter of 1509–10, and the first draft of the work, dedicated to Trithemius, which he had received shortly before 8 April 1510 (SEP). Whether that draft contains III.29 was not checked. The 1531 printings contain Book I only (Wikipedia, 'Three Books of Occult Philosophy').

transmission.work: Polygraphie, et universelle escriture cabalistique (Paris: [Benoît Prévost] for Jacques Kerver)
transmission.author: Trithemius, translated by Gabriel de Collange
transmission.what: The first French translation (Paris: Benoît Prévost for Jacques Kerver, per Sotheby's Tomash lot 669). Wikimedia Commons holds its Theban page as fol. 184v (Boston Public Library copy). The Commons description's English rendering of the French heading names Honorius 'surnamed Thebanus' and his 'rules & ordinances of magic', with no mention of d'Abano, which agrees with a Wikipedia talk-page editor's report that the translation drops d'Abano. The Commons description and From Old Books both report that the final sign is given without the ω and read as an ampersand (&).

transmission.work: Polygraphiae libri sex, later Latin editions (Strasbourg: Lazarus Zetzner), with the Clavis and observations of Adolphus a Glauburg
transmission.author: Trithemius
transmission.what: A Czech library record confirms the Strasbourg (Argentinae) Zetzner edition of 1600, octavo, 612 pp. An NSA pamphlet lists reprints in 1550, 1571, 1600 and 1613 without naming the 1613 printer; Freeman Presson's blog (2014) calls the 1613 edition Zetzner's and places the Theban passage at p. 597. A Wikipedia talk-page editor reports that the 1600 and 1613 reprints keep the final 'w'. None of this was checked against the books.

transmission.work: Three Books of Occult Philosophy (London: R.W. for Gregory Moule)
transmission.author: Agrippa, translated by 'J.F.' (probably John French; NUC also allows John Freake; Wikipedia's citation names 'James Freake')
transmission.what: English text of III.29, with the Theban table re-cut. Wikipedia cites p. 438 (PDF p. 465) of a PDF of the translation; the page in the 1651 printing itself was not checked. The Wellcome record catalogues the translator as 'J.F[reake]', probably John French.

transmission.work: British Library, Sloane MS 3853 (composite magical manuscript)
transmission.author: anonymous compiler
transmission.what: The only known manuscript of Honorius material with the alphabet. It names Agrippa as the source (Wikipedia; Peterson's introduction to the Sworn Book). It shows the alphabet moving from print back into manuscript, not an independent medieval witness.

transmission.work: The Magus, or Celestial Intelligencer (London: Lackington, Allen & Co.)
transmission.author: Francis Barrett
transmission.what: An engraved plate of four registers, with Theban at the top over Celestial Writing, Malachim and Passing the River (Source Library record, whose descriptive fields are machine-generated; it reads the credits as 'Barrett del.', 'Pub. by Lackington & Allen', 'R. Griffith sculp.'). Westcott's Golden Dawn Flying Roll XXXII places the plate facing p. 64 of Book II; Wikipedia cites Barrett, ch. 16, p. 64b. Barrett's book is largely compiled from Agrippa (Wikipedia). Wikipedia names Barrett among the copyists who read the final sign as an ampersand or end-mark. Most modern charts copy this plate. The plate's own caption wording was not seen.

transmission.date: late 19th century (Golden Dawn Second Order period; exact date not seen)
transmission.work: Flying Roll No. XXXII, 'Theban Letters' (Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn)
transmission.author: W. Wynn Westcott (as Frater N.O.M.)
transmission.what: A Golden Dawn instruction paper issued because members asked for the alphabet used on the girdle of the 'Yetziratic image' of Adonai ha-Aretz. It gives the Theban table 'as found in Barrett's The Magus, on the plate facing p. 64 of Book II', traces it through Peter of Abano to Honorius the Theban, and notes that none of the four popes named Honorius was called Theban. It was among the rolls Francis King could not trace; Robert Gilbert later found them in a private collection. Read only through search summaries of online transcriptions.

transmission.work: Draft Unicode proposal for Theban; Unicode mailing-list discussion
transmission.author: Eric S. Raymond (draft); Michael Everson, Kenneth Whistler (replies)
transmission.what: Raymond's draft proposal (catb.org, dated 2002) lists 24 characters and calls them closest to a Latin cipher lacking J, U and W. On the Unicode list (Feb 2002) Everson said he had discussed it with Raymond in 1999 and that its use hardly went beyond ritual objects; he and Whistler treated it as a cypher for Latin. In Nov 2003 Whistler wrote that he found no evidence it had ever been submitted to WG2 or the UTC. The statement that it is still unencoded rests on memory and on its absence from the search results; check the current Unicode roadmap. This is why the site must draw it.

transmission.work: Modern Wicca and popular witchcraft literature
transmission.author: various
transmission.what: Called 'the witches' alphabet'. It is used to write names and words on ritual tools and candles and in personal Books of Shadows (Wikipedia; practitioner sites). Hutton, The Triumph of the Moon (OUP, 1999), records Doreen Valiente's memory of Gerald Gardner (1884–1964) in the early 1950s wearing a silver ring bearing his OTO name in Theban script (wording confirmed in a search excerpt of Hutton's text; page not seen). Wikipedia's 'Gerald Gardner' gives the ring's signs as his witch-name 'Scire' in Theban letters. The route by which the alphabet reached Gardner is not documented in my sources: Barrett's plate was known in the Golden Dawn (Flying Roll XXXII), and blogs suggest that route, but no document shows the transfer.

claims.claim: Honorius of Thebes devised the alphabet.
claims.evidence: Trithemius ascribes the alphabet to 'Honorius cognomento Thebanus' (1518), and Agrippa repeats the ascription (1533). No earlier witness is reported. Who Honorius was is unknown. Wikipedia's account of the Liber iuratus calls its author Honorius of Thebes, 'son of Euclid', and renders his title as 'master of the Thebians'; the book gives no further facts, and its manuscripts do not contain this alphabet (Sloane 3853 apart, which copies Agrippa).
sources: Trithemius, Polygraphia (1518), via Wikipedia and Peterson
Peterson, The Sworn Book of Honorius, introduction

claims.claim: Pietro d'Abano recorded the alphabet in his 'greater fourth book'.
claims.evidence: This is Trithemius's statement ('sicut Petrus de Apono testatur in suo maiore libro quarto'). No such passage is known: Wikipedia says the alphabet is not known to be mentioned in any writing attributed to d'Abano, giving his dates as 1250–1316; Peterson writes that he could not identify any such passage in d'Abano's works and gives c. 1257–1316. Peterson calls the evidence this provides for a historical Honorius 'shaky at best', since writings falsely ascribed to d'Abano are not unknown.

claims.claim: The alphabet was first printed in Trithemius's Polygraphia (1518).
claims.evidence: Wikipedia, German Wikipedia, Peterson and a Pandolfini auction description of the 1518 edition ('the oldest known source of the so-called witches' alphabet') all agree that it is the first printing. Wikipedia's infobox chart is taken from the 1518 book. Unchecked: whether the 1508 manuscript version (ed. Gamer, 2022) already has the table.

claims.claim: Agrippa printed it in De occulta philosophia, Book III, chapter 29.
claims.evidence: The chapter is headed (1651, Peterson's transcription) 'Of the Characters and Seals of spirits'. It says Peter Apponus notes the figures as delivered by Honorius of Thebes. Book III first appeared in the complete edition of July 1533. Pages that give '1531' are confusing it with the 1531 printings, which contain Book I only. Agrippa's Celestial, Malachim and Transitus fluvii are in III.30, not III.29.
sources: Peterson, Esoteric Archives, Agrippa Book III

claims.claim: Trithemius says the alphabet was used to hide 'follies' (fatuitates) in magic.
claims.evidence: The phrase is in the Latin sentence quoted by Wikipedia and Peterson ('cuius ministerio suas in magicis fatuitates abscondit'). It is Trithemius's own, dismissive framing. It is not evidence of how Honorius used the alphabet. I found no source showing that Agrippa repeats the word.
sources: Trithemius, Polygraphia (1518), via Wikipedia 'The Sworn Book of Honorius' and Peterson

claims.claim: The final sign was once a W and became an 'end' mark through misreading.
claims.evidence: As reported, the sign is labelled 'w' (above the sign) in 1518, carries ω and the label Ω in 1533, is read as '&' in 1561, and as an end-mark or ampersand in Barrett. A Wikipedia talk-page editor reports that the 1600 and 1613 Latin reprints keep 'w'. The misreading theory is that editor's. Wikipedia's caption reads the 1533 Ω as 'End'. I did not see the pages.
sources: From Old Books, 'Theban Alphabet of Peter Apponus'

claims.evidence: No exemplar earlier than the 1518 print is reported (Wikipedia). The one manuscript of Honorius material that has the alphabet (Sloane 3853) copies it from Agrippa. The 1508 manuscript version of the Polygraphia was not checked.

claims.claim: Theban is a cipher of the Latin alphabet, not a language or a separate writing system.
claims.evidence: Each sign corresponds to one Latin letter, in Latin order. Peterson calls it 'clearly based on the Latin alphabet, not Greek'. On the Unicode list Michael Everson and Kenneth Whistler treated it as a cypher for Latin (2002, 2003), and Raymond's own draft calls it closest to a Latin cipher.

claims.claim: The Golden Dawn and the OTO used Theban extensively and passed it to Gardner.
claims.evidence: Partly refuted, partly unsupported. Golden Dawn knowledge of the alphabet IS documented: Westcott's Flying Roll XXXII, 'Theban Letters', copies Barrett's plate for members, for the girdle of the Adonai ha-Aretz image. That is one paper, not 'extensive' use. No document seen shows OTO use or a transfer to Gardner. Hutton's report that Gardner's ring bore his OTO name in Theban shows Gardner's own use, not OTO teaching. Others suggest Barrett directly.
sources: Flying Roll XXXII, 'Theban Letters' (Westcott), online transcription
Patheos, 'The Theban Script: (Not So) Secret Alphabet of the Witches' (2016)

claims.claim: Gerald Gardner wore a silver ring with his name engraved on it in Theban letters.
claims.evidence: Hutton, The Triumph of the Moon (1999), records Doreen Valiente's memory of Gardner in the early 1950s wearing a silver ring bearing his OTO name in Theban script (wording seen in a search excerpt of Hutton; page not seen). Wikipedia's 'Gerald Gardner' says the signs represented his witch-name 'Scire' in Theban letters; Hutton elsewhere treats 'Scire' as the magical name Gardner adopted on initiation. Reported as Valiente's recollection.
sources: Hutton, The Triumph of the Moon (OUP, 1999), via search excerpt

letters.name: A
letters.form: NOT DESCRIBED. No image of this sign could be viewed in this environment (1518 Polygraphia, 1533 Agrippa, 1561 French Polygraphie or Barrett's 1801 plate), and no source found describes its strokes in words. It is not described from memory, and nothing about its shape can safely be inferred from its Latin value. Base the drawing on the first printing, Trithemius's Polygraphia (July 1518; Library of Congress Fabyan copy, hdl.loc.gov/loc.rbc/fabyan.17914.1; a crop is on Wikimedia Commons as 'Theban alphabet Trithemius 1518.png', not checked for retouching), and record any variant in Agrippa, De occulta philosophia III.29 (1533; Library of Congress copy, archive.org/details/DeOccultaPhilosophiaLoc1533; Commons file 'Theban alphabet from De Occulta Philosophia 1533.png'). Do not trace the Commons 'cleaned-up' 1518 file (retouched), the 1651 re-cut, Barrett's 1801 plate or modern fonts.
letters.note: Order and value follow the Latin alphabet, to which the table is keyed one sign per letter (Wikipedia; Peterson calls it 'clearly based on the Latin alphabet'). Theban has no numerical values. FACT-CHECK: no form is given, so there is nothing to test against the standard published forms; formConfidence stays low until the sign is traced from the 1518 and 1533 tables.

uses.evidence: Trithemius says Honorius used it to hide his 'follies in magic' (1518, quoted in secondary sources). This describes the purpose Trithemius claims. It is not evidence of medieval use.

uses.use: Modern Wiccan and witchcraft practice ('the witches' alphabet').

The Museum of Witchcraft and Magic (Boscastle) holds a pair of silver-plated chalices inscribed in Theban, 'Circe' and 'Merlin' (object 505). Gardner's ring is reported by Hutton from Valiente. cautions: LETTER FORMS ARE NOT DESCRIBED. Drawing 'Agrippa's Theban' from this file would mean inventing it. Trace the 23 signs and the final sign from the 1518 woodcut, recording the 1533 variants, or show a gap.

Do not say 'Honorius of Thebes invented it' or 'a medieval script'. Say that Trithemius ascribes it to Honorius surnamed the Theban, citing Pietro d'Abano, and that no copy earlier than 1518 is reported.

Do not date Agrippa's printing 1531 (Book I only). Its first printing is 1518 (Trithemius). Agrippa's is July 1533, Book III, chapter 29. Do not confuse III.29 with III.30, which holds the Celestial, Malachim and Transitus fluvii alphabets.
The d'Abano 'greater fourth book' has never been identified. Report it as Trithemius's claim.
Do not give a page number (579 or 597) for the 1518 printing: that printing is unpaginated, and the figures belong to a later paginated edition.
The final sign has four readings: w (1518), Ω/end (1533), '&' (1561) and end-mark (Barrett and modern use). Present it as such. Do not make it a letter in the transliterator.

Theban is not in Unicode (Raymond's 2002 draft was never formally submitted, per Whistler in 2003; current status from memory, check the roadmap), so draw it as vector glyphs. Do not fake it with a font that substitutes Latin letters.
Golden Dawn and Wiccan use should be reported neutrally. Do not reproduce Flying Roll or Book of Shadows texts or any living organisation's emblems.
